hook: Every red wolf on Earth descends from fourteen animals.

story.text: The red wolf is built between its cousins: bigger than a coyote, leaner than a gray wolf, with a reddish tinge behind the ears and down the legs.
It was once the top predator of the American Southeast, from the Gulf Coast to the Ohio Valley.
By the 1970s it was nearly gone, and biologists made the hardest call: catch every last one.
Fourteen of the seventeen captured wolves became founders. Every red wolf alive descends from them.
In 1987, wolves returned to Alligator River, North Carolina — among the first times an extinct-in-the-wild species was rebuilt from captivity.
The population climbed past 130, then collapsed to eight by 2021 — gunshots, vehicles, and coyote hybridization taking wolves faster than they were born.
The rebuilding is intimate: biologists slip captive-born pups, days old, into wild dens, and wild mothers raise them as their own.
As of January 2025, seventeen wild red wolves are known — each wearing an orange collar so drivers and hunters know them.
Behind them stands a captive population of about 250, breeding in zoos across the country.
To witness the red wolf is to keep faith with one of the world's most endangered wild canids, one den at a time.

stats.lifespan: 6–7 years wild · up to 15 in care

reproduction.text: Packs are families: a breeding pair and their offspring, five to eight animals. One litter of three to five pups arrives each spring — sometimes with a zoo-born foster slipped in among them.

insight.text: The red wolf reintroduction became the model — the pilot that paved the way for returning Mexican gray wolves and the wolves of Yellowstone.

programs.title: Red Wolf SAFE breeding
programs.summary: Houses one of the world's largest breeding packs — 42 pups since 2016 — and fosters zoo-born pups into wild dens.
